pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the pantry runs in this workspace. Share it with the operations lead, the warehouse coordinator, the distribution day leads and donor relations.
: each stock line with pounds on hand, the pounds you want on hand, the soonest best-by date and the shelf.
: everything expected and received, with donor, source, pounds and in-kind value.
: each day, its site, lead, volunteers, households served and pounds given out.
: registered households, people in the home, neighborhood, dietary needs, language, last and next eligible visit.
: shelters, senior sites, schools and smaller pantries that pick up food from you.
Donations arrive and are weighed, checked and marked received.
The warehouse coordinator updates stock levels and the soonest best-by date.
Before each distribution day, the day lead checks stock and volunteers.
On the day: open doors, serve households, record households and pounds, mark done.
Partner agencies pick up on their scheduled days.
Every morning: Dashboard, stock below target, food expiring this week
Before each distribution: volunteers confirmed, produce pulled
Every Friday: partner pickups for next week, cooler and freezer logs
Every month: pounds in and out, households served, in-kind value for donor reports
Ask families only what your program needs. Keep the household list private. Let people choose their food where you can; a client-choice table wastes less food and feels better to everyone.
Rename sites, neighborhoods and stock categories to match your pantry, and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.

Most funders ask for the same four numbers: households served, people served, pounds distributed and the value of donated food. The Dashboard charts and the Distribution days and Donations tables give you all four; filter them to the month or quarter you report on.
The pantry at a glance. Charts read the live tables.

text.text: Every pound that comes through the door is weighed, checked and dated before it reaches a shelf. It keeps people safe and gives you the numbers funders ask for.
Expected pickups and drop-offs are on the Donations board as
, with the donor and the stock line they will fill.
Make sure there is room: check the Stock board for the shelf, the cooler or the freezer it needs.
For a big food drive, ask the organizer to sort by type into boxes and to leave out glass, home-canned food and open packages.
Check the temperature of chilled food (41 F or below) and frozen food (solid, 0 F)
Look for dented seams, bulging or leaking cans, torn packages and pests
Check dates; follow your regional food bank's guide for how long past best-by each item is still fine
Turn away anything unsafe and set the donation to
Thank every donor the same week. The

on each donation (pounds times a per-pound rate) gives grocery partners and food drives a number for their own reports; adjust the rate in the formula to match your regional food bank's figure. Large donors get a letter with the total for the year.

First in, first out: new stock goes behind older stock. Write the soonest best-by date on the stock line so the Dashboard shows what to give out first. Produce and dairy go out at the next distribution day.

On Tuesday morning the grocer pickup arrives: 340 pounds of canned vegetables, bread and yogurt. A volunteer weighs each type, finds two bulging cans and discards them, checks the yogurt at 38 F, and marks the donation received. The canned vegetables line moves back to Well stocked, and the yogurt goes straight to the cooler for the afternoon distribution.
Pair a new volunteer with someone experienced for their first two shifts. Lifting rules: bend the knees, two people for anything over 40 pounds, and never stack higher than shoulder height.
A good distribution day feels calm to the families in line: they know where to go, the wait is short, and nobody is made to feel ashamed. The plan below makes that happen.
Check the distribution day on the board: site, doors open time, the day lead and how many volunteers are scheduled.
Look at Stock for anything Low or Out and decide what to substitute.
Pull produce and dairy that must go out first.
Confirm volunteers by text; you need roughly one volunteer for every 15 households expected.
Setup, an hour before doors open
Tables in a loop: check-in, then dry goods, then protein, then produce and dairy
Cooler items stay in the cooler until doors open
Check-in table with the household list, a pen and a translator if one is available
Signs in the languages your households speak (see
when the first family is welcomed
Find the household, confirm the number of people, and note any
New households: register them with only what you need (people in the home, neighborhood, phone). Never ask for more than your program requires.
Households outside the service area are still served today and given the name of their nearest pantry.
Count households served as they pass the last table.
Weigh what goes out, or weigh what comes back at the end and subtract it from what went on the tables.
Watch the line: if it is longer than twenty minutes, open a second check-in.
Return chilled food to the cooler within two hours of doors opening.
Thank the volunteers before they leave.

At the Tuesday evening distribution, 96 households come through in two hours with eight volunteers. The team gives out 2,310 pounds, about 24 pounds per household. Canned protein runs low by the end, so the day lead adds it to the next wholesale order.
Food given out by a pantry has to be as safe as food sold in a store. These are the habits every volunteer learns on their first day.
Fridge and cooler: 41 F or colder. Freezer: 0 F or colder. Check and write the readings at the start and end of every shift.
Chilled and frozen food never sits out more than two hours, and less on a hot day.
If a cooler fails, move the food to another cooler right away, and throw out anything that warmed above 41 F for more than four hours.
Everything at least six inches off the floor and away from the walls
Chemicals and cleaning products stored apart from food, and below it
First in, first out on every shelf
Shelves dry and clean; check for pests weekly
Wash hands before work, after breaks, and after taking out trash.
Gloves when handling unpackaged produce or bread.
Volunteers who are sick stay home: no blame, no exceptions.
Best-by dates are about quality, not safety, for most shelf-stable food. Use your regional food bank's guide. Baby formula is never given out past its use-by date. When in doubt, throw it out.
When a recall notice arrives, search Stock and Donations for the product, pull every unit, and record what you removed. If any went out, contact the households who received it if you can.
Leave food in its original packaging so the label travels with it. Never repack bulk food without writing the ingredients on the new bag.

A volunteer notices the walk-in cooler reads 46 F at the start of the Thursday shift. The day lead moves dairy and produce to the backup fridge, calls the repair company, and checks the log: the reading was 39 F at close the night before, under four hours ago by the door alarm, so the food is kept. The repair is written in the log.
Every volunteer reads this page and signs the shift log. Leads take a food-handler course once a year.
